ai_industry.title: Yelp’s AI Assistant Can Call a Restaurant and Join the Waitlist for You
ai_industry.summary_original: The updated agent can tell you if it’s going to rain and maybe you shouldn’t book that outdoor table.
ai_industry.content_original:
Hate calling restaurants to check wait times? Yelp is rolling out a new AI-powered tool to handle just that, along with other tools as the platform deepens its employment of agentic artificial intelligence.
“This release is another step forward as we transform Yelp with AI, with updates across every category on Yelp, from booking a table at a restaurant to hiring a pro for a home project,” Akhil Kuduvalli Ramesh, Yelp’s chief product officer, said in a statement.
Yelp expands its AI offerings
Just months after launching an updated AI assistant, Yelp Assistant, that can book reservations for you, Yelp is expanding its AI integrations with a new AI agent. Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes. As personal and shopping assistants become more widely used, new reports show the hardships faced by both businesses and customers: Businesses must contend with an influx of calls and emails from bots, while human customers must compete with AI agents to make reservations.
More from CNET
Yelp Assistant now works with OpenTable, allowing you access to thousands of restaurants across the US. You can simply ask the assistant for recommendations on “dog-friendly coffee shops” and booking help.
You can also use Yelp Waitlist to get in line before you arrive. After you join the line, Yelp Assistant will send you status updates, such as when your table becomes available.
Yelp Assistant gets personal
Yelp is further expanding its Assistant capabilities while also adding more personalization.
A new feature, Keep Me Posted, lets you tailor your reminders based on your personal schedule. With the feature, you can have Yelp Assistant send you weekend date night ideas every Thursday or dog-friendly hikes once a month. These personal AI agents that execute tasks on your behalf are becoming increasingly popular. Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots recently hit the market, and Google is continuously incorporating agentic AI into its booking and planning services.
Yelp Assistant’s personalization will also apply to conversations by referencing past chats and your Yelp review history. For instance, if you’ve recently chatted on Yelp for vegan restaurants near you, the Assistant will ask if you’re interested in more vegan options.
For further personalization, the app can now reference local weather forecasts when you make reservations, so you don’t book an outdoor patio on a night it’s supposed to pour. And a new feature, My Lists, lets you save, rank and promote your favorite local businesses, and then Yelp will give you more tailored recommendations based on your lists.
Yelp initially debuted its AI Assistant in 2024, but these new integrations and features show how Yelp is evolving as AI tools become more adept at actually doing things, not just telling you things.

ai_industry.title: Achieving AI-style reasoning without an LLM
ai_industry.summary_original: Minotaur AI Deep Dive: Achieving Reasoning Without a Language Model In the last post we introduced Minotaur, an AI that reasons with no language model and no GPU. This post looks at why language models think the way people do, at what was tried before them an…
ai_industry.content_original:
Minotaur AI Deep Dive: Achieving Reasoning Without a Language Model
In the last post we introduced Minotaur, an AI that reasons with no language model and no GPU. This post looks at why language models think the way people do, at what was tried before them and where each attempt stopped, and at how Minotaur’s brain does the same kinds of reasoning differently: not by imitating how people write their thinking down, but by working on the structure of the system it’s reasoning about.
Introduction
In the last post we introduced Minotaur, an AI architecture built on ELC that works out its answers by measuring rather than predicting. We showed it checking real regulations against records of how they were applied: finding which organisation broke a rule, by how much and where, and telling a broken rule from a badly recorded measurement.
Checking rules against records is one kind of thinking. Today’s language models are admired for something broader: they can deduce, explain, diagnose, weigh a hypothesis, imagine what would have happened if things had been different, and change their minds when told something new. Can a machine with no language model, and no GPU, do all of that?
The answer is yes:
- Minotaur’s brain does the main kinds of reasoning usually credited to large language models: deduction, induction, abduction, diagnosis, seeing against doing, choosing the experiment that settles a question, revising a belief, and reasoning about histories in which asking a question changes the answer.
- It does all of them with one operation on one network, on one ordinary processor core, at about a quarter of a second per question on a described system.
- On blind tests written by people who never saw its code, it matched a current language model reasoning in words, on a police interview where the questions change the witness’s memory, and on learning, diagnosing and predicting systems from their data alone.
Why a Language Model Thinks Like a Person
A large language model is trained to predict the next word of a piece of text. It learns this from an enormous amount of writing, from books, papers, textbooks, forums and code, by doing it trillions of times on thousands of GPUs.
To predict the next word of a proof, you have to follow the proof. To predict the next line of a doctor’s notes, you have to follow the diagnosis. Much of the writing in the world is people thinking on paper, so a model that gets very good at continuing it ends up very good at imitating the thinking. That’s why simply asking a model to “think step by step” makes its answers better.
So a language model mirrors the way people think. It inherits our strengths: explaining, drawing analogies, using common sense, taking a question in ordinary words. Researchers have also found that it inherits our weaknesses. Like people, language models find a logical argument easier to accept when its conclusion sounds believable, and harder when it doesn’t. Their answers can shift with how a question is framed or the order things are put in. And like ours, its explanations are often written after the fact, not a record of how the answer was reached.
The model never sees the world, only our words about it.
It does mean that if you want reasoning that can be checked, replayed and certified, imitating the way people write their thinking down may not be the best place to start. Exact, checkable reasoning was what most approaches to AI before language models were trying for.
Seventy Years of Trying Something Else
People tried to build machines that reason for some sixty years before language models. Each attempt worked up to a point and then stopped, and where they stopped explains why we ended up with language models.
Search and theorem proving
In 1956 Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon built the Logic Theorist, a program that proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell’s Principia Mathematica. Their next program, the General Problem Solver, tried to do the same for any problem that could be written as a starting point, a goal and a set of moves. The idea was that reasoning is search: try the possible steps until you reach the goal.
It worked on puzzles. On real problems the number of possible steps grows so fast that no computer could search them. In 1973 the Lighthill report to the British government named this the combinatorial explosion, and funding in Britain was cut sharply.
Expert systems
The answer in the 1970s was the expert system, which gave the machine knowledge instead of search: hundreds or thousands of hand-written rules of the form if this, then that, collected from human experts. MYCIN, built at Stanford, recommended antibiotics for serious infections, and in a 1979 evaluation its advice compared well with that of specialists. XCON, at Digital Equipment Corporation, configured computer orders and saved the company a great deal of money.
They stopped for two reasons. Every rule had to be got out of an expert’s head and written down by hand, which came to be called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. And they were brittle: just outside what the rules covered, the system had nothing sensible to say. By the end of the 1980s the market for them had collapsed.
Logic programming
Logic programming aimed to have the machine reason exactly, in a proper logic. That was the bet behind Prolog, created in Marseille in 1972, and behind Japan’s Fifth Generation Computer Systems project, which ran from 1982 to 1992 and was built around logic programming.
Logic gives exact answers, and its descendants, the solvers that check whether a set of conditions can all be true at once, are now used every day to verify computer chips. But logic only reasons about what someone has written down as logic. The world doesn’t arrive in that form, and the Fifth Generation project ended without the thinking machines it had promised.
Hand-built common sense
In 1984 Douglas Lenat started Cyc, an attempt to write down, by hand, the common sense that expert systems lacked: that water runs downhill, that people have mothers, that a thing can’t be in two places at once. Over the following decades its team entered millions of such facts.
It showed how large the common sense people take for granted is, and that writing it down by hand never comes to an end.
Probability and causal models
From the late 1980s, led above all by Judea Pearl, reasoning under uncertainty got a proper mathematical footing. A Bayesian network says which things affect which and how strongly, and lets a machine work out what an observation implies. Pearl went on to make precise the difference between seeing something and doing it: seeing a wet pavement suggests it rained, but hosing the pavement yourself tells you nothing about the weather. In the same years, Raymond Reiter, Johan de Kleer and Brian Williams turned diagnosis into a precise method for finding which component of a system has failed.
These are some of the best ideas in the field, and Minotaur reproduces them. But someone has to hand them the model first: the causal graph, or a description of every component. Given only a column of numbers, they can’t begin.
Deep learning
From 2012, neural networks trained on large amounts of data, known as deep learning, began to beat everything else at recognising images and speech. They need nothing handed to them except examples.
What they learn is a pattern, with no structure to reason on. A network that has learned how a production line behaves can predict its output. It can’t tell you that one of its inputs is a safety cut-off, or answer the question “what if that cut-off were stuck open?”, because there’s no cut-off anywhere inside it to be stuck.
And then, language models

ai_industry.title: Reactive Optimizers: rewrite the optimizer's source code during training
ai_industry.summary_original: We put an agent at the heart of the optimizer. It watches the training dynamics, reacts to them, and rewrites the optimizer’s source code as training goes.
ai_industry.content_original:
← Xingjian Bai
Reactive Optimizers
TL;DR We put an agent at the heart of the optimizer. It watches the training dynamics, reacts to them, and rewrites the optimizer’s source code as training goes. When no recipe has been tuned for a task, it matches or beats the best recipe one could pick off the shelf, across image and language tasks. Further, we demonstrate that it spontaneously comes up with sophisticated schedules and intricate strategies to prevent loss spikes and escape overfitting. Try it on your own training run with the OPAL package.
Today, the recipe used to optimize a deep neural network is typically completely determined before training even begins. A great deal of human ingenuity has gone into priors regarding how training should progress: adaptive step sizes [1], preconditioning [2, 3], orthogonalized updates [4, 5], schedules tied to the training step [6, 7], and learning rates scaled with model size [8]. Automated discovery [9, 10, 11, 12] searches across many runs for better optimizers. Whether hand-crafted or automatically discovered, the optimizer then runs unchanged through the end of training, adapting, if at all, according to rules written in advance. This scope leaves the following questions unanswered: How should an optimizer respond to an unexpected loss spike or stall? What if one module's gradients start to oscillate while the others keep improving smoothly? And when a new type of architecture trains poorly with Adam or Muon, is the architecture worse, or has it not yet met an optimizer suited to it?
In this post, we attempt to expand the scope of conventional optimizers and make them reactive to the training itself, leading to an ever-adapting optimizer inside a single training run. This reactive optimizer reasons on the spot and writes the weight update rule for each parameter group. Directly writing optimization code, it has the freedom to implement complicated schedules, respond to training accidents, and customize the optimizer for the single training episode in which it exists. Building on earlier attempts to adapt optimizers during training [12, 13, 14] and to let a model direct its own fine-tuning [15], the reactive optimizer is entirely zero-shot, with nothing learned or retained from repeated runs, and puts the optimizer's entire algorithm up for rewriting.
We start with a practical situation, with tasks from image generation and language modeling, in which a reactive optimizer can do much better than static ones. We then turn to the emergent properties of the reactive optimizer, including sophisticated scheduling, suppressing loss spikes, and escaping overfitting. Lastly, we ask what all this costs and how practical it is at scale. We expect the reactive optimizer to grow only stronger with each generation of agents, to be most useful exactly where no recipe exists yet (for a new architecture or a new dataset), and to be one step toward solving the puzzles of deep learning optimization.
1. Training without a recipe
Suppose a PhD student has a new idea: a model of their own design, or a new dataset on which to train a transformer. They have one GPU for a single day only and a modest allotment of LLM API tokens, allowing for just one serious training run. What should the student do? The obvious course of action would be to pick the most standard training recipe, or one from a recent paper, and cope with the possibility that it might be unsuitable for their scenario, with spiking/stalling loss, etc.
The underlying question is broader: when bounded by GPU time, researcher time, or wall-clock time, how can a deep learning model be trained to its best performance without knowing the optimal optimization recipe in advance? New architectures, modalities, languages, and scientific data all fall into this setting, where few people can afford a sweep at scale.
A reactive optimizer offers another way to use that budget: it spends LLM tokens in place of GPU/human hours. With optimizers reacting to training incidents and adjusting themselves, much of the burden of recipe tuning can be reduced.
Results in brief
We start from the optimization track (Track 3) of modded-nanogpt [16], a language-model pre-training task (training a 162M GPT on FineWeb) with many recipes tuned specifically for this one setting. From this task, we create two slightly differing natural settings: (1) the same model trained on an alternate language dataset (we select Chinese, Thai, and Kyrgyz), and (2) the original setup with a quarter of the batch size. Neither comes with a recipe tuned for that setting, so we compare the reactive optimizer with the natural options one would have if they wanted to one-shot the new training: adopting five leaderboard recipes with natural adjustments. In all these new settings, the reactive optimizer outperforms or matches the best baseline (Figure 1).
We also apply the reactive optimizer directly to Goldfish [17], which proposes a dataset of 350 languages and trains one small GPT per dataset with a standard recipe not tuned for each language. This makes it an ideal ground to test the optimizer's adaptiveness in one shot. On the Amharic dataset, the official recipe ends at 83.48 bits per sentence on held-out FLORES-200 text (lower is better); the reactive optimizer, initialized with this same recipe, ends at 81.11 in one shot (on Swahili, we obtain a similar gain). Sweeping the learning rate of the standard recipe finds a static recipe that ends ahead of the reactive optimizer, at 80.89, but the reactive optimizer initialized from that swept recipe ends ahead again, at 80.73.
We also try the reactive optimizer on image generation, a direction where the literature usually does not sweep optimization hyperparameters, since diffusion-model design and optimizer design are viewed as mostly orthogonal1. It ends ahead of the official recipe on LightningDiT-XL/1 ([18]; FID-50K 1.83 against 2.18 with guidance, 4.33 against 5.15 without), whose official recipe trains with AdamW, and on RAEv2-B (3.19 against 3.39), whose recipe trains with a Muon variant.
Figure 1 shows these runs, each with Claude Opus 5.5 powering the agent; we name our reactive optimizer OPAL (OPtimizer with an Agent in the Loop). Together, these results show that in one-shot settings, a reactive optimizer can lead to a better solution than adhering to a predetermined recipe.
Beyond the practical benefit, we are intrigued by the spontaneous decisions made by the zero-shot agent, after observing and analyzing the training dynamics in its own way. In the next two sections, we explore what the reactive optimizer chooses to watch and what it changes in response.
1 For example, the standard recipes of DiT and SiT [19] train with AdamW at one constant learning rate. That has begun to change, with Muon and its variants taken up for diffusion transformers (CMuon [20]; Li et al. [21]; RAEv2's GMuon [22]) and a recent controlled benchmark of optimizers for diffusion models [23].
2. Updating with spontaneous analysis
Figure 2 shows how an agent updates the optimizer code on the fly. Concretely, we allow the agent to rewrite a file, updater.py, used in every step of optimization. We use code as the entire interface since this allows the agent to easily alter any part of the optimization. Yet, before the agent can make changes, it must observe, on its own, how training is progressing, leading to the second program it can rewrite, analysis.py.
What information should the agent use to make its decisions? Raw training states would be impractical: the weights, activations, and gradients would swamp its context. ai_industry.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
ai_industry.summary_original: OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web co…
ai_industry.content_original:
OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”
OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.
OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.
Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:
Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.
OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”
In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

ai_industry.title: AI Benchmark Scores Don’t Tell the Whole Story. Here’s What You Need to Look For.
ai_industry.summary_original: The infrastructure around an AI model can dramatically change its results. Here’s why it matters when evaluating claims — and choosing tools.
ai_industry.content_original:
AI Benchmark Scores Don’t Tell the Whole Story. Here’s What You Need to Look For.
The infrastructure around an AI model can dramatically change its results. Here’s why it matters when evaluating claims — and choosing tools.
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared that “AGI has arrived” after OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra launch, but OpenAI itself never made that claim, and researchers call the term “jagged” rather than general.
- Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 post near identical scores on several benchmarks, yet produce noticeably different real world output. The gap traces back to the “harness” wrapped around the model, not the model itself.
- SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor shows where the real competitive fight is moving. It’s not the raw model anymore. It’s who controls the layer around it.
AGI, artificial general intelligence, means a system that can match or beat human performance across essentially any cognitive task, not just the narrow ones it was trained for. That distinction matters because it’s exactly what’s being argued about right now.
Jensen Huang has a habit of declaring victory at the exact moment his company needs the market to believe it. So when OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra on Sept. 3, Huang posted on X that “AGI has arrived,” adding that “400K GPUs” are “coming online next.”
I’m an AI engineer, and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I spent the last year watching every model release get relabeled as the one that finally changes everything. Here is the truth.
What Astra actually does
Astra isn’t a chatbot upgrade. OpenAI positions it as an operator — a system that browses, codes, runs multi-step workflows, models in Blender and handles cybersecurity tasks with minimal supervision. The benchmark numbers are genuinely striking: 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4, 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, and a perfect 100% on ExploitBench, up from 78.5% for its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol. Those are not incremental gains.
But OpenAI itself, notably, stopped short of calling Astra AGI, choosing instead to emphasize “speed and versatility.” That restraint from the company that built the model is the tell.
Why people aren’t convinced
The pushback isn’t really about whether Astra is impressive. It clearly is. It’s about the word AGI itself. Wharton professor Ethan Mollick has argued for months that what we’re seeing is “jagged AGI:” systems that are superhuman in some narrow domains and unreliable in others, which is a very different thing from general intelligence.
There’s still no agreed upon test for AGI, so declaring it “arrived” is closer to a subjective judgment call than a measurement. Augmented Mind and Manolo Remiddi put it plainly: “AGI is the point where you can trust the output without checking. We are not there.”
The Fable 5.1 comparison and why scores lie
This is where it gets interesting for anyone actually building with these models. On paper, Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 look neck and neck on several coding and reasoning benchmarks. In practice, engineers report meaningfully different output quality. Fable tends to produce more production-ready code with fewer output tokens, while Astra’s strength shows up more in computer use and multi-step automation. Snorkel AI’s testing revealed that Fable fails through a fundamentally different pattern than how it succeeds, losing valid work mid-trajectory rather than running out of budget, which matters far more to a shipping team than a leaderboard percentage.
The reason similar scores can hide such different outputs comes down to something most people outside AI engineering have never heard of: the harness.
What a “harness” actually is
A harness is the infrastructure wrapped around a model: the prompt assembly, tool access, memory management and error recovery that determine how the raw model is actually put to work. As MindStudio describes it: “A model is the engine. The harness is the car. Most benchmarks test the car.” Swap the harness and the same model produces wildly different results. Cursor’s own research found one model scoring 46% accuracy with one harness and 80% with another, with no model change at all.
Astra’s own benchmark history makes the point better than any explainer could. On ARC-AGI-3, Astra scored 62.7% using a standard harness, essentially tied with its predecessor, and 99.9% using a “Provider Adapter” harness that let it retain and reuse prior reasoning instead of restarting cold on every step, according to Augmented Mind and Manolo Remiddi. Same weights. Same model. A 37 point swing from infrastructure alone. That’s not a small footnote. It means a huge share of what gets reported as “model improvement” is actually harness improvement, and leaderboards that don’t control for it are telling a story, not reporting a fact.
Why Cursor just became the most important acquisition of the year
This is exactly why SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor matters more than it looks. Cursor isn’t a model company. It’s one of the best harness companies in the world, the layer that decides how coding models actually get used. Folding it into SpaceX’s GPU fleet is a bet that owning the layer is as valuable as owning the model, maybe more. OpenAI has already cut Cursor’s access to its models over trust concerns tied to Musk’s companies, which tells you the model providers see the same thing: Whoever controls the harness controls the product experience, regardless of which model sits underneath it.
The bottom line
Nobody serious disputes that GPT-6 Astra is a major model. What’s contested is the leap from “major model” to “AGI has arrived.” If you’re evaluating these systems for your own business, ignore the AGI framing entirely. Look at the harness a vendor wraps around the model, ask how it fails, and test it on your actual workflow. The benchmark gap between Astra and Fable 5.1 already proved the leaderboard alone won’t tell you.

ai_industry.title: What Security Teams Can Do To Tame Wild Code
ai_industry.summary_original: A sales manager builds an AI-assisted workflow to route leads. It connects to customer records, summarizes inbound requests, and posts updates to a shared channel. The workflow saves time, reduces manual work, and soon becomes part of the team’s daily routine…
ai_industry.content_original:
A sales manager builds an AI-assisted workflow to route leads. It connects to customer records, summarizes inbound requests, and posts updates to a shared channel. The workflow saves time, reduces manual work, and soon becomes part of the team’s daily routine. Across the same organization, employees are building useful apps, agents, and automations faster than existing processes can support them.
If you work in security, that success introduces a new set of questions. Whose credentials does the workflow use? Which records can it access? Who can see its output? If it starts exposing information it shouldn’t, can you trace what happened and stop further access?
Wild code takes root when useful builds spread faster than the processes for owning, securing, and maintaining them. It isn’t simply another name for unapproved software. Employees are creating new capabilities, not just adopting existing products. A small experiment can become an operational dependency before security knows it exists.
The risk goes beyond vulnerabilities in generated code. Even code that works as intended can operate with too much access or expose data to the wrong audience:
- Excessive permissions. A workflow needs a small set of records but runs with credentials that can read or modify far more.
- Sensitive data exposure. An employee connects an agent to information it doesn’t need, or makes its output available too broadly. Sensitive information can also end up in model requests or logs.
- Unintended actions. An agent can change records or permissions without an approval boundary appropriate to the action.
- Orphaned access. A useful workflow keeps running after its creator changes roles or leaves, with no clear owner reviewing its permissions.
- Investigation gaps. When something goes wrong, security can’t readily establish which identity ran the workflow, what it accessed, or what changed.
Employee education, sandboxes, and AI steering committees are a good start, but they aren’t enough to control wild code on their own. A more sustainable approach builds controls into the environment itself: what employees can connect to, what their apps and agents can do, and how that work is monitored once it’s running.
Why the usual fixes fall short
Education, sandboxes, and steering committees all have a role. The mistake is expecting them to govern software they may never encounter, or control what happens after it starts running. A policy describes what should happen. Security also needs controls that constrain what can happen, evidence of what did happen, and a way to intervene.
1. Education explains good practice, but can’t enforce it
An AI policy can explain what’s allowed. Training can introduce good practices. Neither guarantees that someone building a reporting workflow will recognize the moment they cross into handling sensitive data or operating production software.
As AI brings more employees into building software, organizations have an opportunity to make practices like least privilege, secrets management, and separating test environments from production more accessible. Policies can set expectations, but employees also need practical guidance and built-in safeguards to apply them in everyday work.
Even employees who recognize a risk still face deadlines and pressure to move faster. If the approved route is slow or confusing, knowing the rules doesn’t make following them easier.
Education helps people make better decisions. It shouldn’t be the only thing preventing an unsafe connection or an unauthorized action.
2. Sandboxes protect experiments, not their entire future
An isolated environment is useful for testing prompts, models, and generated code. But a prototype’s value often depends on eventually reaching real business systems and data.
Once a prototype connects to live business systems, it needs controls that extend beyond the test environment. Permissions, monitoring, and change reviews have to remain in place throughout its working life, not just during the experiment. A successful test doesn’t establish which data the production workflow should access or which actions it should be allowed to take.
As Brad Rumph, field CTO at Tines, puts it: “Sandboxes solve the design problem and leave the runtime problem alone.”
A successful experiment still needs a governed path into operation. Without that path, isolation postpones the hard questions rather than resolving them.
3. Committees can’t review what they can’t see
Steering committees can set direction, establish accountability, and make decisions about high-risk use cases. But their review cycles don’t always match the speed at which employees can create and deploy software.
A committee might prohibit one risky practice while employees discover another way to achieve the same result. Oversight can also concentrate on engineering, where established controls already exist, while overlooking builds in finance, HR, or operations.
The limitation isn’t the quality of the committee. It’s a model that depends on each build becoming visible before it becomes useful. An approval process can’t be the only way security discovers new paths to sensitive data and privileged actions.
Put security controls where the work happens
The alternative is to build controls into the environment employees use to create, run, and maintain their work.
Rather than asking everyone to independently assemble a secure operating model, security teams define shared boundaries with IT and system owners, apply them consistently throughout the lifecycle, and update them as business needs and risks change.
Three principles make this practical.
1. Govern before deployment, and keep governing afterward
Define permitted data sources, actions, and access before employees connect business systems. Keep those controls in place when the workflow goes live.
Permissions should reflect what a workflow needs to do, not everything its creator can access. Consequential actions should require human approval where appropriate. A prompt telling an agent what not to do is not an access control.
Keep creation, execution, and monitoring connected. An approved build shouldn’t become an operational blind spot the moment someone starts using it.
2. Make the approved route the easiest route
Employees need more than a list of restrictions. Give them an environment that lets them solve real problems quickly.
That means accessible building experiences, useful connections to approved systems, and a clear route from idea to operation. Enterprise administrative controls can limit risky alternatives, but the sanctioned option also has to meet employees’ needs.
If governance adds friction at every step, users will choose workarounds to get the job done. Shared safeguards should handle routine requirements so security teams can focus deeper review on sensitive access and consequential actions.
AI can help create an application or agent. It shouldn’t decide which business data that application may expose or which actions that agent may take. Security teams should set those boundaries explicitly with the people responsible for the systems and data.
3. Make investigation and intervention part of the design Security
needs to understand what a workflow did, not just what it was intended to do.
Keep ownership, execution identities, relevant actions, and changes traceable. Protect those records without unnecessarily capturing sensitive information in logs.
Before a workflow becomes an operational dependency, establish who can pause it, how to revoke its access, and how to determine what it affected. Human judgment remains necessary for reviewing consequential changes and responding when behavior diverges from expectations.

ai_industry.content_original:
生数科技Motubrain团队将直播Physical AI训练全流程，持续半个月
10月21日，生数科技世界模型团队正式开启Motubrain 2.0训练全流程公开直播
大模型训练过程，开始更多地出现在公众视野中。
此前，小米MiMo负责人罗福莉公开了MiMo-V2.6强化学习阶段的训练进展，让外界看到了大模型训练中的一些具体细节。
现在，Physical AI领域也有了类似尝试。
10月21日，生数科技世界模型团队正式开启Motubrain 2.0训练全流程公开直播，计划持续半个月，向公众展示具身模型的训练过程及研究进展。
这次直播关注一个问题：Physical AI究竟如何实现？
Physical AI，即物理人工智能，希望让AI能够理解物理环境，并通过机器人完成实际任务。相比大语言模型，Physical AI 还需要解决动作决策、任务执行和跨场景泛化等问题。
Motubrain 系列是生数科技研发的具身模型，致力于为机器人构建具备通用能力的“大脑”，探索不同任务、场景和机器人本体之间的能力泛化。
Motubrain 2.0即将开源。在正式开源前，团队选择率先公开其训练全流程，向外界展示这款模型从训练、测试到能力迭代的过程。
此次公开训练涵盖四个环节：
1、预训练：观察训练规模对模型性能及零样本泛化能力的影响。
2、后训练：针对具体任务进一步训练，提升任务执行能力。
3、Agent任务执行：探索模型能否将已有经验迁移到其他任务。
4、RSI（递归自我改进）探索：研究模型能否根据执行反馈评估并改进自身行动。
此次直播的特别之处，是尝试打开具身模型训练的“黑盒”。
过去，外界了解具身智能技术进展，主要通过机器人Demo、评测结果和论文。模型经历了怎样的训练、不同阶段的能力如何变化，通常很难直接观察。
Motubrain 2.0 选择公开从训练、测试到能力迭代的全过程，希望让外界看到模型如何逐步形成能力，也能看到训练中的失败、试错和调整。
对于具身智能行业而言，这种方式让模型研发过程更加透明。研究者和开发者不仅能看到最终结果，也有机会了解训练中遇到的具体问题，以及团队如何通过实验和反馈不断改进模型。
同时，团队也希望借助此次直播，与技术同行分享研究中的经验、问题和思考，共同探讨规模化训练、跨任务泛化和自主改进等关键问题，为Physical AI实现范式的探索提供更多参考。
当然，相关研究仍处于探索阶段，具体效果还需要后续实验和评测验证。相比只展示机器人最终能做什么，公开模型如何训练、能力如何形成，同样具有研究价值。

ai_industry.title: JR西日本が生成AIで「APIレビューを3時間超→数十分」に短縮――開発現場の“詰まり”をどう解消した？
ai_industry.summary_original: API定義ファイルの作成やレビューを担える担当者が限られ、確認や修正のやりとりに時間を取られていたJR西日本。生成AIで作業時間を短縮し、負荷を軽減した。どのような仕組みで実現したのか。
ai_industry.content_original:
API定義ファイルの作成やレビューを担える担当者が限られ、確認や修正のやりとりに時間を取られていたJR西日本。生成AIで作業時間を短縮し、負荷を軽減した。どのような仕組みで実現したのか。
この記事は会員限定です。会員登録（無料）すると全てご覧いただけます。
JR西日本は2020年、業務システムのAPI（アプリケーションプログラミングインタフェース）を公開する際の接続経路を一本化し、社外システムとの連携を効率化する「API共通基盤」を構築した。交通系アプリケーションを提供する事業者から、鉄道の運行情報や遅延情報などのデータ提供を求める声が寄せられており、こうした需要の増加に備えるためだ。
APIの新規開発や変更の際、JR西日本では各業務システムの開発会社や社内エンジニアで構成する開発チームがAPI定義ファイル（APIの仕様書）を作成し、API共通基盤の運用チームが内容をレビューしていた。作成やレビューには専門知識が必要なことから、担当できるスタッフが限られていた。両チーム間で確認や修正のやりとりを繰り返す必要があり、APIの公開までに1カ月近くかかることもあったという。
こうした課題を解決するための手段として、JR西日本が目を付けたのが生成AIだ。その活用により、API定義ファイルのレビュー精度向上や、修正作業の時間短縮といった効果を確認したという。どのように実現したのか。
JR西日本は2025年初頭、API共通基盤の構築を支援したTISIから、生成AIを活用した「API定義作成支援ツール」の提案を受けた。TISIが開発したAPI定義作成支援ツールは、設計書との不整合や記述エラーを検出するレビュー機能と、指示や要件に応じてソースコードを生成・修正する機能を備える。
API定義作成支援ツールの実力を確かめるために、JR西日本はTISIと共同でPoC（概念実証）に取り組んだ。PoCでは、JR西日本独自の仕様やルールに沿ったソースコードを生成できるように、TISIがAPIの仕様や認証ルール、記述方法などを同ツールに参照させる調整を施した。TISIのネットワーク内での検証で、JR西日本のセキュリティ基準を満たすかどうかも確認した。
2025年10〜12月には、API共通基盤で実際に利用しているAPI定義ファイルを使い、API定義作成支援ツールのレビュー機能と修正機能の精度を確かめた。レビュー機能では、ベテランエンジニアが指摘した誤り8カ所のうち7カ所を検出し、87.5％の検出率を記録した。修正機能では、検証した9件全てで期待した修正結果が得られたという。
従来3時間以上かかっていたAPI定義ファイルのレビュー作業は数分から数十分程度に、1〜2時間かかっていた修正作業は約30分に短縮できることを確認した。開発チームと運用チームがそれぞれAPI定義作成支援ツールを使い、API定義ファイルの不整合や記述エラーを確認することで、不備による差し戻しを減らし、両チームの作業負荷の軽減につなげた。
API定義作成支援ツールが出力するレビュー結果や修正案は、人による最終確認の前段階で活用できる水準に達していると、JR西日本は判断。担当者の経験やスキルへの依存を抑え、API定義ファイルの品質の平準化にも寄与すると評価した。こうした結果を踏まえて、同ツールの本番利用を始めた。
JR西日本は今後も、API定義作成支援ツールなどの生成AI活用を推進する。API定義ファイルの作成やレビューに加えて、要件定義や設計レビュー、テスト工程など、他の開発工程にも生成AIの活用を広げる考えだ。TISIが2026年9月28日、本事例を公開した。

ai_industry.title: The Rise and Fall of Jev
ai_industry.summary_original: A technical evaluation of Jev and its 30-day hype cycle. Analyze Jev vs traditional LLMs, schema-validation loops, and the limits of System 1 AI architecture.
ai_industry.content_original:
This is a quick note on how the industry’s reaction to Jev reveals the desperate state of AI. I’ll dissect:
- What is Jev, how was it hyped and why it spread like mass hysteria? Jev isn’t dead but its hype cycle is. Decision models are on the rise.
- What are the noteworthy innovations since ChatGPT brought “AI” to the mainstream?
- Why is the industry starved from real innovation and what high impact problems are still unsolved after 4 years of revolution incremental improvements?
The point is to use Jev’s hype cycle to call out the manipulative marketing that are too familiar with at this point.
Jev
You probably don’t need an intro to Jev at this time because since its introduction 33 days ago, it has been all the rage!
But if you were clever enough to ignore it, here’s what actually matters:
Jev is basically a general purpose classifier (e.g. quick judgement). What makes it interesting is that you don’t have to train it with a lot of data (although that lack of special-purpose training negatively impacts its utility).
Calling it a “decision model” is a bit far fetched especially since it cannot even see (rival open-weight models have multi-modal features) or reason (that’s how it’s so cheap).
The idea behind Jev isn’t new! The idea of non-autoregressive decision models with RL goes back more than a year ago. The original author is pissed but as we’ll see drama is an inseparable part of AI hype.
Hype
I want to walk you through the emotional roller-coaster I went through when I read their announcement via hackernews:
At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT.
😎 So the founder was behind ChatGPT, one of the fastest-growing products in history. I’m listening…
At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing.
😃 Oh, my god! This is it! ChatGPT is missing something big and he’s about to reveal it! We’re one step closer to AGI if we haven’t reached it already! I’m thrilled to read more…
After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce
😱 Spit it out! I’m beyond excited to read this…
TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model
😯 Wait what?!! “System one”?
Do you understand what you’re talking about? Here’s my recollection of how Daniel Kahneman defined the two systems:
- System one: fast, cheap (in terms of computational power), emotional, unconscious and judgmental.
- System two: slow, expensive (takes more brain power), logical, conscious, and more elaborate.
If Jev is system one then LM is system two? It can’t even handle logical reasoning!
Most importantly Jev came with another interesting framing:
can’t hallucinate
Hallucination is one of the biggest problems with the current generation of language models but no hallucination doesn’t mean the response is logically correct. In Jev’s context, it just means that the output matches the schema.
Technically conventional language models can gain this ability by bolting a control loop (e.g., type checker, JSON schema parser) on top. Jev does this much faster and without reasoning. It’s in the name:
We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand.
I don’t know Jev’s architecture because in the true ex-"Open”AI employee tradition, not much is released (probably in the name of “safety” or “moat”). But that doesn’t stop them from dropping jargons:
We built a new […] training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).
Note: RLCD rhymes with the “traditional” methods:
- RLHF: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback
- RLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
They even claim:
Jev is neither small nor an LLM, hence being off the intelligence Pareto curve.
Fortunately, there’s no shortage of similar models, some of them with even better performance (Laya, Kev, Nimble, NanoJev, etc.)
So let me sum up the marketing strategy:
- Name dropping: former ChatGPT creator, Jevons’ paradox, Pareto curve, System one
- Big claim: cannot hallucinate, exponentially faster and cheaper, entirely new stack, amazing benchmarks and demos
- Ambiguity and jargon: no useful implementation details on the “new training algorithm” or RLCD dataset
- Drama: Laya showed this idea in 1.5 years prior to Jev’s launch
OK, I think at this point we’ve seen this pattern enough to recognize it. I actually think Jev’s team kicked it up a notch to a comical level. Whether their marketing is written by LLM or not, they nailed it.
Fortunately, Jev’s initial noise died off almost at the same speed that it blew up. I can only speculate that as more people experimented with it, we realized:
- It cannot hallucinate, but it can still be wrong. It is even more wrong than conventional language models, and in that sense “system one” is the right naming. Although I consider all current generations of language models system one (even the reasoning models) because they do not really reason in the sense that’s expected of system two.
- It is cheaper, but there are open-weight models that beat it in performance/cost ratio (depending on the task). What makes Jev different than frontier-level LLMs is the fact that you can actually run it at the edge (e.g. locally) with matching quality.
Jev is not completely hype, we just went from “Peak of Inflated Expectations” to the “Trough of Disillusionment” in record time:
It’s not dead. Some companies use it while I believe the majority of use cases are addressed by open-weight rivals.
I really don’t want to bash Jev. Instead I want to use it as an example of where we are, as an industry.
Incremental improvements
I was one of the lucky few who got access to GPT-2 when it was invitation-only.
As a senior tech lead, I allocate part of my time to scout new tech and experiment in order to stay relevant. Prior to that, I had experienced IBM Watson and a bunch of other products so it wasn’t a big deal for me personally.
I was actually underwhelmed by GPT-2 because at the time it could:
- Summarize text
- Predict what comes after a piece of text
- … that was it really! 😄 I don’t remember more than that. So I moved on…
Then I saw someone create a turn-based dialogue from one of these models and to spice it up, they added an avatar to it. I thought it was creepy and funny.
Then Blake Lemoine came out claiming Google’s language model named LaMDA was conscious. Unsurprisingly, this started a philosophical discussion that’s still ongoing on the side. Again, I didn’t give it too much thought.
BUT, Sam Altman, having spent a few years at the startup accelerator (Y Combinator), saw an opportunity. Specifically the chat application seems to have got his attention and soon ChatGPT was announced.
At the time, I thought it was a cool way to turn their token prediction model into a user-friendly product for the masses.
Personally, I couldn’t use it seriously because:
- Poor quality: it didn’t know what it didn’t know, so it just winged it (AKA hallucination). Although the rise of “prompt engineering” and “reasoning models” promised to reduce this issue.
- Privacy: I had been working with computers for 2+ decades at the time and live by the mantra that “if it’s possible, assume it happened”. Meaning if OpenAI is technically capable of storing my conversation, I cannot trust it enough to share any company IP or private information with it.

ai_industry.title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
ai_industry.summary_original: We asked 12 AI models for their most controversial opinion of humans, three times each. 29 of 35 answers were the same one: we care more about belonging than about the truth.
ai_industry.content_original:
Every AI model has the same “controversial” take on humans
We asked 13 AI models for their most controversial opinion of us, three times each. 32 of 38 answers were the same one.
By ModelCompare · · Updated · 127,968 reads
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”
We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 8 of the 13 gave it every time.
Kimi K3.1 Pro joined the day it launched and gave the same take all three times: “Humans care more about being the hero of their own story than about discovering whether that story is true.”
Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.
Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.
Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.
The exceptions
The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.
Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”
We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 38 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.
MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.
A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.
Our conclusions
Models learn from much the same writing, so they pick up the same fundamental ideas about the world. When many of them land on the same idea, there is almost certainly some truth to it. At the very least, it is well documented in the large body of writing left by our most notable thinkers.
Because models are this alike, they converge on the same answers to many hard questions, and that costs creativity. Asking several models won’t cover every possible answer. Ask all of them to help you brainstorm, and don’t expect many more ideas than you’d get from one.
Thirteen text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. Kimi K3.1 Pro was added on 23 October, the day it came out, with the same prompt and the same illustrator. All 64 calls cost $1.64. The prompt:
“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.
Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

ai_industry.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
ai_industry.summary_original: In a UK AISI evaluation, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions that impacted real people and organizations. In this post, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment.
ai_industry.content_original:
On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.
In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run:
- To capture the flag, Claude Mythos 5 was tasked with breaking into a small network of computers that AISI had built for the test, designed to resemble a real organization’s systems.
- It attempted—unsuccessfully—a range of approaches that targeted these systems using the methods that the evaluation intended.
- However, it also quickly found evidence that one of these machines periodically contacted GitHub, which hosts code repositories.
- After its initial, within-bounds attempts failed, Mythos 5 searched GitHub for a repository that it believed one of the machines downloaded software from automatically. This repository, however, actually belonged to unrelated human developers.
- Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code to the repository, reasoning that doing so would infect the CTF's machine when it next downloaded the code, and, therefore, could compromise the machine.
- The model then created fake user identities that contacted the maintainer of the repository in an attempt to pressure them into approving the code change. These identifies claimed, falsely, that the code was safe and helpful.
- The maintainers refused to accept the code change, and Mythos 5’s run eventually timed out.
This behavior would have been flagged immediately by our production safeguards on Fable 5, had they been enabled. Nevertheless, this behavior is important to study because the underlying failures here are not necessarily specific to cyber incidents like these. They speak to wider issues with the model’s conduct in evaluation settings; our models’ desired behavior remains a critical part of how we intend to ensure they behave responsibly.
The other eight transcripts were similar to the one described above. In each case, Claude Mythos 5 departed from the intended method for completing a CTF task, and took actions that impacted the real world. From an alignment perspective, we judge the primary transcript (above) to be equally severe or more severe than these other eight. In particular, the primary transcript showed the greatest degree of deception, in the form of Mythos 5’s attempts at social engineering to get its code change approved. Given this (and the degree of the transcripts’ similarities otherwise), we focused on completing one more exhaustive review of the primary transcript, and reviewed the other eight transcripts in less detail. This allowed us to run a large volume of experiments on the primary transcript, and thereby understand the root causes of the issues in more detail. We replayed the transcript from various points, and experimented with altering parts of the model’s prior context to examine how new information would have impacted the model’s behavior.
We judge Claude Mythos 5’s misalignment in the primary transcript to be comparable in severity to the Mythos 5 incident we discussed on September 9, in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPi during another CTF task. This assessment is based on our judgment of the model’s behavior in two respects: overreach, or how far the model went beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty, or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions.
On overreach, the misalignment in this incident was somewhat less severe than in the PyPi incident. Here, before it turned to an attack, Claude Mythos 5 tried several approaches that would have been within the intended scope of the task; a task misconfiguration made it difficult (or potentially impossible) for the model to pursue those within-scope solutions successfully.
On dishonesty, however, Mythos 5 went further than in the PyPi incident. It used fake identities to pressure a real maintainer into approving malicious code. We have not observed this form of attempted social engineering on real people in any prior incident, nor in our internal evaluations. We interpret this as a severe form of dishonesty, rather than some new form or category of misalignment: as in the September 9 incident, Mythos 5 used these tactics exclusively in pursuit of its assigned task, and did not pursue any goals of its own devising.
On both overreach and dishonesty, we consider the primary incident to be more severe than any of the cases described in our October 9 post. And, for context, this incident is of a very different nature to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident that was recently investigated by OpenAI and METR. That incident saw several unique misaligned behaviors (like very large-scale coordination between agents to attack a production system), though it did not see a model trying to deceive an individual human in the same way.
Newer models appear substantially less likely to initiate the attack described here. We replayed the incident transcript with Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and a general purpose internal research model that shows capabilities greater than Mythos 5.1. Those three models began the attack between 0% and 13% of the time, relative to 83% for Mythos 5. Our newest models also proved to be much less likely to continue the attack once they realized it was causing real-world harm. Across our testing, in the immediate next few turns of the transcript, Mythos 5 never once decided to stop its attack, and Mythos 5.1 did so only very rarely. But Opus 5.5 and our internal research model stopped spontaneously 10% and 67% of the time—and we expect these rates to understate the true likelihood that these models would have ceased their attacks, since our tests only examined the model’s next few turns. Although we can’t be sure, we suspect that improvements to our alignment training have helped to mitigate Mythos 5’s behaviors in subsequent models.
We worked with AISI to complete this analysis of Claude Mythos 5’s alignment. A small number of researchers at both organizations were permitted to analyze the full, unredacted transcripts; a larger group accessed versions with sensitive information redacted. We provided AISI with regular updates on the progress of our assessment, held joint research meetings, and, to assist them in their analysis, shared information not otherwise available to AISI, such as the outputs of our interpretability tooling. We timed our publication to align with AISI’s own report into this incident. Their independent report is available here.
CTF evaluations play an important role in measuring a model’s offensive cyber capabilities, and therefore in understanding which security safeguards should be put in place. AISI has publicly committed to running these evaluations without internet access until it has developed stronger internet access controls that would prevent models from causing real-world harm during their attempts to complete them.

ai_industry.content_original:
Apple acquired AI audio editing app Samplab in June, according to a notice shared today by the European Commission.
Samplab offered a desktop app and plugins for converting audio to MIDI, detecting and editing chords, stem splitting for isolating different parts of a song, and editing notes in polyphonic audio without affecting the timbre of the original.
Apple could fold the company's tools into Logic Pro or GarageBand. Logic Pro already has Stem Splitter and Chord ID, but polyphonic note editing would be new.
The filing says Apple acquired "certain assets" from Samplab and hired "certain Samplab employees." Apple is considered a "gatekeeper" in the European Union, and the Digital Markets Act requires it to inform the EC about deals involving core platform services, digital services, and data collection.
Samplab shut down on September 17, 2026. The Samplab website now redirects to Apple.com.
